title: 1627-drawdown-risk-beyond-brownian-motion
universal_lens: Drawdown risk is formalized as a functional over stochastic return paths, mapping non-Gaussian archetypes to quantile distributions of maximum drawdown and recovery time. This unifies Brownian benchmarks with trended or mean-reverting dynamics under a single Monte Carlo stress-testing manifold.
gsi_mapping: GSI employs conformal inference on simulated path ensembles to construct distribution-free prediction intervals for bankroll drawdowns. By treating Sharpe ratios and Hurst exponents as calibration parameters, GSI maps archetype-specific tail risks into robust Bayesian credible sets for future losing streaks.
gse_mapping: GSE integrates the Monte Carlo drawdown-quantile framework to dynamically adjust state transitions during prolonged losing streaks. The engine maps discrete pick-level P&L to continuous archetype proxies, using block-bootstrap corrections to enforce conservative bet-sizing when empirical returns deviate from Gaussian assumptions.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core mathematical derivation stems from recognizing that standard Brownian motion severely underestimates drawdown risk when returns possess memory or heavy tails. By constructing a Monte Carlo manifold of return paths—spanning pure Brownian, trended, mean-reverting, and market-neutral archetypes—we derive quantile distributions for critical drawdown statistics like maximum loss and recovery time. These statistics are normalized by annual volatility and indexed by Sharpe ratio, revealing that mean-reverting/short-volatility strategies suffer significantly higher 90th-percentile drawdowns (2.48 vs 1.87 for Gaussian). To bridge simulation and reality, the framework introduces a stationary block bootstrap coupled with Hurst-exponent stress testing (H=0.5 to 0.7). This allows GSE to map its discrete, time-varying pick-level P&L onto these continuous archetypes, applying a non-Gaussian correction factor to its bankroll management. The dualities lie in translating continuous-time financial mathematics into discrete sports betting sequences, while failure modes arise if the empirical edge exhibits rapid, unmodeled regime switches that violate the assumed archetype stability.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This lineage traces back to Feller’s excursion theory and Lévy’s work on Brownian motion extrema, later adapted by Mandelbrot for fractional processes. In quantitative finance, it evolved through the study of value-at-risk under fat tails. Here, it retroactively informs sports betting by importing rigorous drawdown quantile analysis from continuous trading to discrete event markets, correcting naive Gaussian assumptions. reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: We model the opposing agent—the sportsbook or market—as an entity that implicitly prices in non-Gaussian risks, particularly during trending periods or volatile line movements. The decision actor (GSE) must anticipate that their edge may behave like a mean-reverting or short-volatility strategy, facing clustered losses. By adopting this adversarial view, GSE proactively scales back bet sizes when empirical Hurst exponents suggest persistent negative autocorrelation in their pick returns.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A veto is triggered if the block bootstrap yields highly collinear paths with the base Gaussian assumption, indicating no significant memory effect. Furthermore, leakage occurs if the simulation uses future knowledge of line adjustments; thus, we strictly enforce causal ordering in the P&L generation. If the empirical drawdown exceeds the 90th percentile of the most stressed archetype (mean-reversion), the system halts aggressive staking until the regime reverts to stationarity.
